LOCKDOWN POLICE BRUTALITY

By: Ntokozo Miya | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
Throughout the lockdown, we have seen reports of people being wrongfully arrested for contravening the Disaster Management Act. In many cases, people are reprimanded and arrested even when they have done nothing wrong. For example, our case studies include a man who was arrested on his way to buy electricity at a nearby shop, people who were arrested while walking or jogging on the beach during the allocated exercise time between 6am and 9am, and a father who was fined when he collected his children from his parents' home in Mpumalanga after the lockdown extension.

We investigate the validity of these arrests and the apparent abuse of power by law enforcers in some of the cases as well as the implications of the criminal records attached to these cases. We also dissect the difference between an admission of guilt and bail – we spoke to people who honestly believed they were paying bail when they were in fact admitting that they were guilty and getting a criminal record.

One of our case studies helps illustrate that despite the government assuring them that the relevant department were aware of the changing regulations, the information doesn't filter to some enforcers on the ground – after parents were granted permission to move their children from one province to another, law enforcers told our parent they knew nothing of the sort, and then slapped him with R2000 rand fine.

Also, in the KZN incident captured on video, with the father in a scuffle with police over his child, we have learned that the incident was a climax to a situation that was brewing earlier. It turns out that the father was one of eleven people taking in by police after being "caught" walking on the beach during exercise time with his child. The father was among the parents who asked to leave their kids at home before being taken in to the police station for processing. While doing exactly this, he has no idea why the police suddenly went for his son. This is when the video was taken.

Further information:
We not only speak to victims who were either arrested or paid admission of guilt fines but also, a family in Aliwal North where a mentally challenged mother was severely beaten and has been in police custody since April 12. Police have refused to say what she is charged with, details below under case studies.

Script:


FINAL LOCKDOWN ARRESTS

UPSOUND
Collins Khosa SANDF video
VO – This was the scene in Alexandra on the 10th of April after an altercation between resident Collins Khosa and security officers enforcing lockdown regulations.
UPSOUND – COURTESY STRAP - CB APRIL 2020 ARCHIVE
VO - “... when soldiers allegedly spotted Collins Khosa enjoying a beer in his yard on Good Friday, they accused him of breaking lockdown rules. It is reported that the soldiers then assaulted Collins so severely, he later died.
NOSIVIWE MAPISA-NQAKULA – DEFENCE AND MILITARY VETERANS MINISTER
... In such cases, obviously the law will take its course.”
VO – A subsequent South African National Defence Force inquiry found that its members had only pushed and slapped Khosa, actions they said could not have caused his death.
The investigation is ongoing.
In the court ruling that ordered the probe, Judge Hans Fabricius noted that the very institutions created to “protect the population... now fail to impose the appropriate internal remedies against the transgressors.”
UPSOUND - Videos of lady being pepper sprayed and the guy being beaten up by police and SANDF inside yard
VO – Such clashes led to the United Nations condemning the militaristic response to the pandemic, putting South Africa among the top fifteen most problematic countries for heavy-handed enforcement.
BHEKI CELE – MINISTER OF POLICE
I'm giving the number of 243 146 people that have been arrested.
VO – Two months into lockdown, Police Minister Bheki Cele's arrest figures show a huge spike, from just over seventeen thousand in the first week – which makes arrests for minor infringements a great concern.
LINK - Who would have thought that exercising, buying electricity or fetching children from grandparents would get you a criminal record - some South Africans arrested during lockdown say they were doing essential tasks permitted by government.
VO – On the 28th of March, Ebrahim Hartley of Mitchells Plain in the Western Cape went to the shops to buy bread and electricity.
EBRAHIM HARTLEY – MITCHELLS PLAIN RESIDENT
Down the street, there was a lot of police vans picking up people. The officer grabbed my arm and he pulled me to the van.
VO – At the Mitchell's Plain police station, Ebrahim produced a slip with his meter number and a twenty rand note, the exact amount for the items he needed.
EBRAHIM HARTLEY – MITCHELLS PLAIN RESIDENT
But they didn't want to hear anything. They were just booking me, taking fingerprints.
VO – Ebrahim was charged with contravening the Disaster Management Act and is due in court next month.
A guilty verdict could tear the family apart as Ebrahim and his wife Rushaan are in the process of adopting a four-year old boy.
RUSHAAN HARTLEY – MITCHELLS PLAIN RESIDENT
It's going to make things difficult for that if he's got a criminal record.
VO – Mitchells Plain police directed our inquiry about Ebrahim's arrest to the national department. The department had not responded at the time of this broadcast.
Under lockdown level four, walking and jogging was permitted between 6am and 9am, however, that exercise was not to take place in parks or at the beach.
Glad she and her husband could resume their morning walk routine, Marijke Lord of Ballito in the KwaDukuza Municipality in KwaZulu-Natal says they went for stroll on the 10th of May around 7.30am.
MARIJKE LORD – BALLITO RESIDENT
I was on the path that leads down to the beach when we were arrested.
VO – The path is about one hundred metres away from the beach and yet, municipal officers accused the couple of having actually been on the beach.
MARIJKE LORD – BALLITO RESIDENT
We did get to a point where we were requested to pay bail. It was a thousand rand per person.
VO – Over and above having spent a day in these cells, Marijke and her husband now have the threat of criminal records hanging over their heads.
BHEKI CELE – MINISTER OF POLICE
We are in discussion with the minister of justice on these matters to see how people that have committed petty crimes do not find themselves with criminal records.
LINK - Experts say considering the tensions of the pre-democratic era in South Africa, it's understandable that law enforcers and the public often have tumultuous interactions whenever they face off.
VO – Psychologist Professor Malose Langa explains that the lockdown has brought back traumatic memories of the past.
PROF. MALOSE LANGA – COMMUNITY-COUNSELLING PSYCHOLOGIST
The image of police and soldiers is that of violence. Permits amount to what under apartheid was called dompas for you to have permission to walk here.
VO – Police brutality was evident in the case of Sipho Hlahla who lives with his 55-year old mother Alina in Aliwal North in the Eastern Cape.
SIPHO HLAHLA – ALIWAL NORTH RESIDENT
She started to be a little bit mentally disturbed in January 2007. That was the time she lost her job.
VO – Alinah has no comprehension of the stay-at-home regulations. On the 12th of April, she came face-to-face with police while walking around her neighbourhood.
SIPHO HLAHLA – ALIWAL NORTH RESIDENT
They started beating her. They told me my mom is arrested because she assaulted the police but she was full of blood. There was no police who was beaten by my mom.
VO – When we met Sipho, his mother had already been detained for six weeks.
Following Carte Blanche enquiries to the Eastern Cape police, Alina was released just days before this broadcast. Brigadier Tembinkosi Kinana said police were not initially aware of her mental condition.
BRIGADIER TEMBINKOSI KINANA – EASTERN CAPE SAPS

The lady started hurling insults at the police in an uncontrolled way. She resisted arrest, however the police managed to overpower her.
VO – Kinana would not be drawn to comment further on the alleged assault as the case has been referred to IPID.
BRIGADIER TEMBINKOSI KINANA – EASTERN CAPE SAPS
She has been released on warning so that she could be brought to an institution for psychiatric examination.
VO – The use of excessive force is a blatant violation of human rights, insists Khuselwa Dyantyi of SERI, the Socioeconomic Rights Institute.
KHUSELWA DYANTYI – SOCIOECONOMIC RIGHTS INSTITUTE
Our very fundamental rights, even during this lockdown, cannot be suspended. You cannot take away my dignity.
VO – IPID, the Independent Police Investigative Directorate, is investigating three hundred and seventy-six complaints in which officers are accused of misconduct including brutality and causing death.
But SERI researcher Thato Masiangoako worries IPID's independence is questionable, and its conviction rate isn't very encouraging.
THATO MASIANGOAKO – SOCIOECONOMIC RIGHTS INSTITUTE
There's only been about just over 1% of a successful criminal conviction of a police officer. IPID is tasked to investigate the police but also has to report to the police.
VO – IPID spokesperson Sontaga Seisa argues their conviction rate might be low but they do thorough investigations.
SONTAGA SEISA – IPID
I can't tell you why are we reporting to the same police minister. The IPID Act is before the parliament. We're hoping that it is going to give us more independence, structurally and operationally
VO – Abuse of power by police can extend into how they apply the law. Wynand Blignaut from Kempton Park in Gauteng, felt confident to fetch his children from their grandparents in Middelburg, Mpumalanga when travel restrictions were temporarily relaxed.
On his way, he was stopped at a roadblock by the Ekurhuleni Metro police department, EMPD.
WYNAND BLIGNAUT – KEMPTON PARK RESIDENT
They pulled me over asking me for the permit. I said no I don't have a permit. I'm going to collect the kids in Middelburg. No, you're not allowed, you need a permit.
VO – But there is no specific permit for collecting children from another province. Wynand had with him other documents.
WYNAND BLIGNAUT – KEMPTON PARK RESIDENT
The birth certificate, proof of residence, our marriage certificate, both ID's. We took everything.
VO – Wynand was served with a two thousand rands traffic fine but was allowed to proceed to Mpumalanga.
WYNAND BLIGNAUT – KEMPTON PARK RESIDENT
I did everything by the book and still they just abused their power.
VO - The EMPD said it would investigate the complaint.
LINK - Some people say they were scared and bullied into paying an admission of guilt fine at the police station, which they did just so they could get back home to their families.
VO – Admitting guilt allows offenders to pay a fine to avoid a trial and jail time.
KHUSELWA DYANTYI – SOCIOECONOMIC RIGHTS INSTITUTE
Once you pay, that means that is going to your criminal record. You will be having that criminal record for your life.
PROF. MALOSE LANGA – COMMUNITY-COUNSELLING PSYCHOLOGIST
Images of prisons are highly, highly traumatic and then you begin to worry – so the only way out is if I admit to guilt.
VO – Deputy Minister of Justice and Correctional Services, John Jeffrey, warns against admitting guilt if you have not broken the law.
JOHN JEFFREY – DEPT. OF JUSTICE AND CORRECTIONAL SERVICES
There is an amendment on the cards to basically providing for you not to get a criminal record in most admission of guilt matters, not all. But as things stand currently, you will get a criminal record.
VO – Though his mother will not be getting a criminal record, Sipho is not satisfied that the officers who allegedly assaulted her have not been held accountable.
SIPHO HLAHLA – ALIWAL NORTH RESIDENT
The police beat the woman but they always preach that you can't beat a woman but they did that.

PROMOS

Arrested while buying bread and electricity – South Africans detained during lockdown worry that they went out to perform essential tasks but may have come back with criminal records.

South Africans arrested during lockdown say they were just going out to get essential items when they were detained by law enforcers who accused them of minor infringements.

Allegations of brutality and abuse of power by law enforcers – we investigate if South Africa's response to the Covid-19 pandemic isn't too militaristic.

VO – But there is no specific permit for collecting children from another province. Wynand had with him other documents. WYNAND BLIGNAUT – KEMPTON PARK RESIDENT The birth certificate, proof of residence, our marriage certificate, both ID's. We took everything. VO – Wynand was served with a two thousand rands traffic fine but was allowed to proceed to Mpumalanga. WYNAND BLIGNAUT – KEMPTON PARK RESIDENT I did everything by the book and still they just abused their power. VO - The EMPD said it would investigate the complaint. LINK - Some people say they were scared and bullied into paying an admission of guilt fine at the police station, which they did just so they could get back home to their families. VO – Admitting guilt allows offenders to pay a fine to avoid a trial and jail time. KHUSELWA DYANTYI – SOCIOECONOMIC RIGHTS INSTITUTE Once you pay, that means that is going to your criminal record. You will be having that criminal record for your life. PROF. MALOSE LANGA – COMMUNITY-COUNSELLING PSYCHOLOGIST Images of prisons are highly, highly traumatic and then you begin to worry – so the only way out is if I admit to guilt. VO – Deputy Minister of Justice and Correctional Services, John Jeffrey, warns against admitting guilt if you have not broken the law. JOHN JEFFREY – DEPT. OF JUSTICE AND CORRECTIONAL SERVICES There is an amendment on the cards to basically providing for you not to get a criminal record in most admission of guilt matters, not all. But as things stand currently, you will get a criminal record. VO – Though his mother will not be getting a criminal record, Sipho is not satisfied that the officers who allegedly assaulted her have not been held accountable. SIPHO HLAHLA – ALIWAL NORTH RESIDENT The police beat the woman but they always preach that you can't beat a woman but they did that. PROMOS Arrested while buying bread and electricity – South Africans detained during lockdown worry that they went out to perform essential tasks but may have come back with criminal records. South Africans arrested during lockdown say they were just going out to get essential items when they were detained by law enforcers who accused them of minor infringements. Allegations of brutality and abuse of power by law enforcers – we investigate if South Africa's response to the Covid-19 pandemic isn't too militaristic.

metadata.Summary: Throughout the lockdown, we have seen reports of people being wrongfully arrested for contravening the Disaster Management Act. In many cases, people are reprimanded and arrested even when they have done nothing wrong. For example, our case studies include a man who was arrested on his way to buy electricity at a nearby shop, people who were arrested while walking or jogging on the beach during the allocated exercise time between 6am and 9am, and a father who was fined when he collected his children from his parents' home in Mpumalanga after the lockdown extension. We investigate the validity of these arrests and the apparent abuse of power by law enforcers in some of the cases as well as the implications of the criminal records attached to these cases. We also dissect the difference between an admission of guilt and bail – we spoke to people who honestly believed they were paying bail when they were in fact admitting that they were guilty and getting a criminal record. One of our case studies helps illustrate that despite the government assuring them that the relevant department were aware of the changing regulations, the information doesn't filter to some enforcers on the ground – after parents were granted permission to move their children from one province to another, law enforcers told our parent they knew nothing of the sort, and then slapped him with R2000 rand fine. Also, in the KZN incident captured on video, with the father in a scuffle with police over his child, we have learned that the incident was a climax to a situation that was brewing earlier. It turns out that the father was one of eleven people taking in by police after being "caught" walking on the beach during exercise time with his child. The father was among the parents who asked to leave their kids at home before being taken in to the police station for processing. While doing exactly this, he has no idea why the police suddenly went for his son. This is when the video was taken.
metadata.Further information: We not only speak to victims who were either arrested or paid admission of guilt fines but also, a family in Aliwal North where a mentally challenged mother was severely beaten and has been in police custody since April 12. Police have refused to say what she is charged with, details below under case studies.
